summary: Describes the preferred design of a Pseudowire Emulation Edge-to-Edge control word for use over an MPLS network, along with the pseudowire associated channel header. The fields are chosen so a label switching router that inspects payloads will not mistake a pseudowire payload for an IP packet. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4385 defines headers that help MPLS routers recognize pseudowire traffic instead of mistaking it for IP. The preferred control word can also carry a sequence number so a receiver can detect packets that arrive out of order.

subtitle: Headers that help MPLS routers distinguish pseudowire traffic from IP packets.

tldr.problem: MPLS does not identify the payload protocol in its standard encapsulation. A router inspecting payloads can mistake pseudowire traffic for IP and send packets along different paths.
tldr.mechanism: The pseudowire control word starts with four zero bits, while the associated channel header starts with four one bits. The preferred control word also includes flags, a length and a sequence number.
tldr.outcome: The headers distinguish pseudowire data and associated-channel traffic from IP payloads and can support sequencing. RFC 4385 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 5586.

facts.label: Control-word sequence number
facts.value: 16 bits; values 1 to 65535, with 0 meaning not used

today: RFC 4385 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 5586. It has not been obsoleted according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: Why Pseudowires Need a Distinguishing Header
sections.content:
A pseudowire carries one kind of traffic across an MPLS packet-switched network. Standard MPLS encapsulations do not include an explicit protocol identifier, so a label-switching router inspecting the payload may mistake pseudowire data for an IP packet.

If a router uses payload inspection to choose an equal-cost path, packets from one pseudowire may take different paths and arrive out of order. RFC 4385 defines headers that distinguish pseudowire data and associated-channel traffic from IP.
sections.plainLanguage: An MPLS router may inspect a packet to choose a path. A distinguishing header helps it recognize pseudowire traffic and avoid treating it as IP.

sections.title: The First Four Bits Identify the Header
sections.content:
IPv4 and IPv6 packets begin with version values 4 and 6. A pseudowire packet carried over MPLS MUST NOT begin with either value in its first four bits. A first nibble of 0000 identifies a PW MPLS Control Word; 0001 identifies a PW Associated Channel Header.

The control word is for pseudowire data. The associated-channel header is for traffic such as Operations, Administration and Maintenance (OAM). The selected header must immediately follow the bottom of the MPLS label stack.
sections.plainLanguage: The first four bits tell a router whether the packet carries pseudowire data or associated-channel traffic. Neither defined value looks like an IPv4 or IPv6 version field.

sections.title: The Preferred Control Word
sections.content:
The generic control word begins with four zero bits; the pseudowire encapsulation defines the remaining 28 bits. The preferred format uses four flag bits, two fragment bits, a six-bit length and a 16-bit sequence number.

The length helps the receiving provider-edge router remove padding added by an Ethernet segment. If the MPLS payload is under 64 bytes, the length field contains the pseudowire payload and control-word length; otherwise it is zero. The fragment bits are used when fragmenting a payload.
sections.plainLanguage: The preferred control word has fields for signaling, fragments, length and packet order. Its length field helps a receiver remove padding in small MPLS payloads.

sections.title: How Sequence Numbers Work
sections.content:
When sequencing is enabled, the sender starts at sequence number 1 and increments for each packet. After 65535, it returns to 1. If sequencing is not supported or enabled, the sender sets the field to zero.

The receiver expects sequence number 1 initially. Zero means it cannot determine packet order. A packet within the allowed window of 32768 may be treated as in order; other out-of-order packets may be dropped or reordered at the receiver's discretion.
sections.plainLanguage: When sequencing is active, each packet carries a number that increases from 1 through 65535 and then starts again. The receiver uses the numbers to identify packets that may be out of order.

sections.title: The Associated-Channel Header
sections.content:
The associated channel carries traffic alongside user traffic so both follow the same path through the packet-switched network. Its header is four bytes long and begins with 0001. It contains a version field, a reserved field and a 16-bit channel type.

This RFC defines version 0. Senders must set the reserved field to zero, and receivers ignore it. The channel type comes from an IANA registry; the RFC identifies 0x21 for IPv4 and 0x57 for IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: The associated-channel header identifies special traffic that travels with the pseudowire data. Its channel-type value says what kind of traffic the channel carries.

sections.title: Protecting Associated-Channel Traffic
sections.content:
An application using the associated channel must consider how an attacker could disrupt a pseudowire, affect a provider-edge router or use the channel to deliver packets elsewhere. This RFC leaves the choice of security mechanism to the application.

If a pseudowire is configured without a control word, the associated-channel mechanism MUST NOT be used. Otherwise, a user payload could imitate the associated-channel header and reach the application that handles that channel.
sections.plainLanguage: An application that uses the associated channel must protect it from misuse. The channel must not be used when the pseudowire has no control word.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Per-payload signaling defined by the pseudowire specification.

fields.name: FRG
fields.desc: Used when fragmenting a pseudowire payload.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Payload plus control word length for MPLS payloads under 64 bytes.

fields.name: Sequence number
fields.desc: Packet sequence number; zero means sequencing is not used.

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: Version defined by this RFC is 0.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Sent as zero and ignored on reception.
